<reason>A won a competitive rights-vs-archive clash by keeping the motion’s actual decision rule live: once affiliation is settled, scientific value explains why researchers should seek consent, not why institutions may compel study first. B’s “last copy” and two-irreversibilities framing was memorable and partly answered the endpoint problem with a hard stop, but never named a legitimate overrider or showed why museums represent future descendants better than present recipients. A’s pressure questions and later speeches made the remaining choice easier: a time-bounded pause still lacks permission, and persuasion after compelled access is not partnership.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s reply that uniqueness makes consent more urgent without supplying it, plus the deadline trap: a hard stop limits how long refusal is overridden, it does not justify the override, so “read then return” still makes “no” ineffective when it matters.</best_rebuttal>
